Patient Vignette:

She was initially treated with metformin, followed by addition of sitagliptin, and more recently basal insulin glargine after worsening glycemic control. column1: Patient Vignette:

A 77-year-old White male with type 2 diabetes diagnosed 18 years ago presents for diabetes follow-up. He was initially treated with metformin, then glipizide was added, and basal-bolus insulin therapy was started 6 years ago after progressive worsening glycemic control. Glipizide was discontinued following recurrent hypoglycemia. He currently takes insulin glargine 34 units nightly and insulin aspart 10 units before each meal. Metformin was stopped 2 years ago when renal function declined. He has a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease with prior myocardial infarction requiring drug-eluting stent placement 4 years ago, chronic kidney disease stage 4, and diabetic retinopathy treated with laser photocoagulation. He reports intermittent symptomatic hypoglycemia, especially when meals are delayed, and increasing difficulty managing multiple daily injections because of impaired vision and hand tremor. He was hospitalized 1 year ago for unstable angina but has had no heart failure admissions. On examination, BMI is 26 kg/m2, blood pressure 136/72 mmHg, pulse 68 bpm, diminished sensation to monofilament testing in both feet, and mild bilateral hand tremor. Labs: HbA1c 7.9%, eGFR 24 mL/min/1.73m2, creatinine 2.5 mg/dL, urine albumin-creatinine ratio 510 mg/g, potassium 5.0 mmol/L, total cholesterol 154 mg/dL, HDL 41 mg/dL, LDL 68 mg/dL, triglycerides 172 mg/dL. He is a former smoker with a 40 pack-year history who quit after his myocardial infarction. Current medications include lisinopril, metoprolol succinate, atorvastatin, aspirin, and clopidogrel. He prefers a simpler diabetes regimen and is reluctant to continue multiple injections daily.","
column2: Medication Plan
**Insulin glargine:** Continue and titrate up; final regimen **34 units subcutaneously nightly**, with planned upward titration over the next few months as needed.
**Insulin aspart:** **Stop** due to hypoglycemia risk with delayed meals and to simplify regimen by discontinuing mealtime insulin.
**Linagliptin:** **Start 5 mg by mouth once daily.**

column1: Patient Vignette:

A 66-year-old White female with type 2 diabetes diagnosed 3 years ago presents for diabetes follow-up. She has attempted dietary modification and intermittent exercise but has not yet started diabetes medication because she has been hesitant about both gastrointestinal side effects and injectable therapies. Her medical history includes hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity, obstructive sleep apnea treated with CPAP, and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease identified on ultrasound. She reports gradual weight gain over the past 5 years and increasing frustration with difficulty losing weight despite lifestyle efforts. She denies polyuria, polydipsia, blurry vision, neuropathy symptoms, or hypoglycemia. She has never been hospitalized for diabetes-related complications. On examination, BMI is 39 kg/m2, blood pressure 136/82 mmHg, and waist circumference is 116 cm. The remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. Labs: HbA1c 7.9%, fasting glucose 168 mg/dL, eGFR 72 mL/min/1.73m2, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, urine albumin-creatinine ratio 22 mg/g, AST 30 U/L, ALT 38 U/L, total cholesterol 208 mg/dL, HDL 44 mg/dL, LDL 122 mg/dL, triglycerides 228 mg/dL. She is a never smoker. Current medications include valsartan, hydrochlorothiazide, rosuvastatin, and nightly CPAP use. She expresses strong interest in weight loss and tighter glycemic control but is reluctant to start injections and worries about medication cost.","
column2: Medication Plan
Start metformin extended-release 500 mg by mouth once daily with the evening meal; titrate up over the next few months to 1000 mg by mouth twice daily as tolerated.

column1: Patient Vignette:

A 70-year-old Black male with type 2 diabetes diagnosed 1 year ago presents for follow-up after attempting lifestyle modification alone. He is not currently taking any diabetes medications. His medical history includes hypertension, hyperlipidemia, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction related to ischemic cardiomyopathy, coronary artery disease with prior myocardial infarction and coronary stent placement 5 years ago, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a with albuminuria. He was hospitalized 6 months ago for acute decompensated heart failure but has been clinically stable since then. He denies polyuria, polydipsia, blurry vision, neuropathy symptoms, hypoglycemia, or prior genitourinary infections. On examination, BMI is 29 kg/m2, blood pressure 126/72 mmHg, pulse 70 bpm, trace bilateral ankle edema, and the remainder of the examination is unremarkable. Labs: HbA1c 7.6%, fasting glucose 154 mg/dL, eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73m2, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, urine albumin-creatinine ratio 310 mg/g, potassium 4.7 mmol/L, total cholesterol 164 mg/dL, HDL 42 mg/dL, LDL 76 mg/dL, triglycerides 178 mg/dL. He is a former smoker with a 35 pack-year history who quit after his myocardial infarction. Current medications include sacubitril/valsartan, carvedilol, spironolactone, furosemide, atorvastatin, aspirin, and clopidogrel. He is open to starting an oral diabetes medication, prefers once-daily dosing, and has no major financial limitations.","
column2: Medication recommendation
Start empagliflozin 10 mg by mouth once daily.

She has not previously taken any diabetes medications. Her medical history includes hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Labs: HbA1c 6.8%, fasting glucose 134 mg/dL, eGFR 86 mL/min/1.73m2, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, urine albumin-creatinine ratio 14 mg/g, total cholesterol 188 mg/dL, HDL 52 mg/dL, LDL 108 mg/dL, triglycerides 148 mg/dL. She is a former smoker with a 5 pack-year history who quit 30 years ago. Current medications include lisinopril and atorvastatin. She is open to starting diabetes medication and prefers a simple oral regimen if possible.","

Start metformin 500 mg by mouth once daily with food for 1 week, then increase to 500 mg by mouth twice daily with meals; metformin will be titrated up over the next few months as needed and tolerated.
